desc: This station involves taking a history from the carer of a child with intellectual disability and acute behavioural change, and explaining to the examiner the approach to assessment and management.
explain:
Behavioural change in a child with intellectual disability

Children with intellectual disability often cannot describe pain or discomfort, so distress is expressed through behaviour. A sudden change (aggression, self-injury, withdrawal, sleep or appetite change) should prompt a search for a physical cause first, rather than being attributed to the disability or to "challenging behaviour" (diagnostic overshadowing).

What to look for

  • Physical causes: pain (including dental), constipation, reflux, UTI, endocrine problems such as thyroid disease, epilepsy, sensory problems, sleep disorders. Ask carers about bowel habit specifically, as constipation is common and often missed.

  • Medications: review for side effects and polypharmacy. Antipsychotics such as risperidone can cause extrapyramidal effects (stiffness, tremor, drooling, akathisia), constipation, sedation and weight gain. Akathisia can itself look like agitation and lead to further dose escalation.

  • Psychosocial factors: abuse, neglect, carer stress, and recent changes such as the loss of a trusted support person, new routines or transport changes.

  • Talk to the patient directly using simple language, gestures and visual supports, and always include their carers' observations.

In this case

Liam has faecal loading (made worse by risperidone, low fluids and low fibre) and a dental abscess or caries, both painful. His risperidone was increased and he shows extrapyramidal features. He has also lost a trusted aide. All of these plausibly contribute to his behaviour, and a behaviour plan or further antipsychotic would address none of them. Management includes disimpaction with a maintenance osmotic laxative, urgent dental care and analgesia, a medication review in liaison with the prescriber, support for the school transition and carer support.

The SDQ

The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire is a brief behavioural screening questionnaire for children and adolescents with parent and teacher versions. It covers emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactivity/inattention, peer problems and prosocial behaviour. It is a screening and monitoring tool, not a diagnostic test, and is only interpretable once physical and situational causes have been considered.
focus: Child with intellectual disability and behavioural change
guide:
A high-performing candidate would talk to Liam as well as the parent, and recognise early that a sudden change in behaviour in a child who cannot communicate should be treated as pain or illness until proven otherwise. They would ask about bowels, teeth, reflux and urinary symptoms, review the risperidone dose increase and its extrapyramidal and constipating effects, and sensitively screen for abuse, neglect, carer stress and recent changes in routine such as the loss of the teacher's aide. They would describe a full examination including abdomen, mouth and skin, treat constipation and dental pain, and address medication before any behavioural intervention. They would explain the SDQ as a brief parent and teacher behavioural screening tool covering emotional, conduct, hyperactivity/inattention, peer and prosocial domains, and place it after the medical assessment.

A borderline candidate would take a history focused on the behaviour alone, accept the school's framing and move towards a behaviour plan, SDQ or psychiatry referral without searching for pain, constipation or medication effects. They may not talk to Liam, may overlook the risperidone dose change, and may give an incomplete or incorrect description of the SDQ.
patient:
Profile:

  • Relationship: Parent of Liam Nguyen, aged 10.

  • Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander: No.

  • Setting: GP clinic or paediatric outpatient clinic. Liam is present in the room, sitting with a tablet, and is not able to answer questions.

Presenting complaint: "He has become so angry and aggressive. The school says he needs a behaviour plan, but this isn't like him."

History of presenting complaint:

  • Onset about 3 weeks ago, gradual worsening.

  • Hitting staff and other children at school, throwing objects, screaming in the afternoons.

  • Hitting his own abdomen with his fist and pressing his belly against the edge of furniture (disclose only if asked about self-injury or what he does when upset).

  • Pulls at the side of his face and refuses to eat crunchy foods; has been chewing less (disclose only if asked about eating or face/mouth behaviours).

  • Sleep disrupted, waking crying at night, 3 to 4 times a week.

  • Appetite reduced over the past fortnight.

  • No fever, no vomiting, no cough. No obvious injury or fall.

Bowel and bladder (disclose only if specifically asked):

  • Bowels open every 4 to 5 days, hard pellet stools, strains and cries. Soiled underwear twice in the past week (parent thought this was "him being naughty"). Previously opened bowels daily.

  • Slightly more wetting than usual; no change in urine smell or colour. Parent is unsure if he has pain passing urine.

  • Drinks little water; fussy diet, low in fibre.

  • Occasionally arches his back and brings up food after meals (reflux history since infancy, no current treatment).

Medications:

  • Risperidone 0.5 mg twice daily, started by a previous specialist 8 months ago for aggression. Dose increased 6 weeks ago. Parent has noticed he is stiffer, drools more and seems restless, unable to sit still (disclose if asked about medication side effects or changes).

  • Melatonin 2 mg at night.

  • Parent is not aware that risperidone can cause constipation.

Background:

  • Moderate intellectual disability, cause unknown (previous genetic testing normal). Born at term. Mild reflux in infancy.

  • No known epilepsy. Immunisations up to date.

  • Last dental check was more than 2 years ago because he does not tolerate it.

  • Allergies: nil known.

Social (disclose when asked about changes at home or school):

  • Lives with both parents and a younger sister. Parent is tired and says they are "at their limit" with the lack of sleep, but denies any harm to Liam and no concerns about anyone else caring for him.

  • 4 weeks ago his favourite teacher's aide, who he had worked with for 3 years, left the school. A new relief aide has been working with him.

  • No change in routine at home, no new carers, no unexplained bruises. Liam is not fearful of any particular person.

  • School bus driver changed at the same time.

Parent's concerns: Wants the behaviour to stop and is worried they will be asked to keep Liam home from school. If the candidate suggests it may be a physical cause: "Do you really think he might be in pain? He can't tell us."

Cues:

  • If the candidate speaks to or engages Liam directly (greeting, explaining, using simple language or gestures), Liam calms and looks at them.

  • If the candidate blames the parent or labels Liam as "behavioural", the parent becomes upset.

Use only the provided history. The candidate should use non-medical language; interrupt if medical jargon is used.

Examiner information (provide when the candidate asks about examination findings):

  • Temperature 36.8 °C, HR 100/min, RR 20/min, BP 100/60 mmHg, weight stable.

  • Abdomen: distended, firm faecal loading palpable in left iliac fossa and suprapubic region, mildly tender, no peritonism.

  • Mouth (limited view): poor dental hygiene, large carious lower right molar with gum swelling and tenderness.

  • Mild cogwheel rigidity in the upper limbs, mild tremor, restlessness (akathisia).

  • Perianal inspection: no fissure; skin normal. No bruising or injuries on skin survey.

  • Urine dipstick: leukocytes negative, nitrites negative, glucose negative.
points: In a child with intellectual disability who cannot report symptoms, a sudden behavioural change is pain or illness until proven otherwise: look for dental pain, constipation, reflux, UTI and endocrine causes.

Always review medications for side effects (for example extrapyramidal effects and constipation with antipsychotics) and polypharmacy, and consider abuse, neglect, carer stress and recent changes such as losing a support worker.
Ask carers specifically about bowel habit and speak to the patient directly.

The SDQ is a brief parent/teacher behavioural screening questionnaire covering emotional, conduct, hyperactivity/inattention, peer and prosocial domains; it is not diagnostic and does not replace a medical assessment.

stem:
You are a general practitioner (or a paediatric registrar in an outpatient clinic). Liam Nguyen, a 10-year-old boy with moderate intellectual disability, is brought in by his mother/father. He is largely non-verbal and uses a few single words and gestures.

The parent reports that over the past 3 weeks his behaviour has become much worse. The school has suggested he needs a behaviour management plan and has asked the parent to complete a Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ).
tasks: Take a focused history from the parent (5 minutes).
Tell the examiner your assessment, including what you would do on examination and which investigations you would consider (2 minutes).
Explain to the examiner the role of the SDQ and your initial management plan (1 minute).
